This page contains a collection of common misconceptions, frequently
asked questions and concerns about preregistration. This page is
designed to be used as a reference guide and the collection is organized
according to the stages of doing a preregistration. The colored tags
indicate the topic the question falls under.

## Thinking about doing a preregistration

**The data I use comes from a large database, can I still preregister my
study with existing data?**

[Study
type]{style="background-color: #2b66ff; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}
[Practical]{style="background-color:  #cc0066; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
Yes, with some additional considerations needed.

Increasingly researchers conduct new analyses on existing data from
large-scale databases. The analytical decisions made for pre-existing
data can be influenced quite strongly by a researcher's prior knowledge,
which can contribute to questionable research practices.

@vandenakkera provide a template and a detailed worked example for how
to carry out a preregistration for pre-existing data. Some additional
considerations covered in the template are "What prior knowledge do you
have about the dataset that may be relevant for the proposed analysis?".
:::

**My study is descriptive (e.g. observational), is doing a
preregistration still useful?**

[Study
type]{style="background-color: #2b66ff; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
There are cases where preregistration might not be appear to be
applicable, however descriptive studies can be preregistered! You can
preregister research questions, modelling approach and data
wrangling/analysis steps. It can also be helpful to find examples of
preregistered studies with a similar research approach to you to get an
idea of what it can look like in practice (e.g. see descriptive
preregistration [example](https://osf.io/7qpa8/overview)).

See this commentary by [@dal-ré2014] for more information about
preregistration of medical observational studies.
:::

**What is the difference between a preregistration and a registered
report?**

[Terms and
concepts]{style="background-color: #3abf57; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
Registered reports are a publishing format where a study undergoes *two
stages* of peer review:

- *stage 1:* introduction and methods in advance of data
  collection/analysis and

- *stage 2:* which includes the full study findings including
  results/discussion [@parsons2022].

Registered reports have been described in the literature as "Two-stage
review with in-principle acceptance" [@mayo-wilson2025].
:::

**Is it true that doing a preregistration increases the risk of being
scooped?**

[Practical]{style="background-color:  #cc0066; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}
[Ways of
working]{style="background-color:  #f9c002; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
The fear of scooping is understandable given the current competitive
research culture of "publish or perish". Preregistrations do not need to
be made public right away and can be embargoed for a period of years
(e.g. [Open Science Framework
preregistrations](https://help.osf.io/article/634-addressing-fear-of-scooping-on-osf-preregistrations)
can be embargoed for 4 years from first submission). The embargo period
allows you time after preregistering your study to conduct the research,
analyze, write up and publish the findings.
:::

## Preparing a preregistration

**I am keen to try out doing a preregistration but my supervisor thinks
it is a “waste of time”, what should I do?**

[Ways of
working]{style="background-color:  #f9c002; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
Often a reluctance to try out preregistration comes from a place of lack
of familiarity with the process. Sharing resources, and suggest a group
meeting to discuss/learn more about preregistration to increase
familiarity. Reframe preregistration as a creative opportunity to plan
great science! Planning is where the science is, as other research
processes, like data collection can be delegated.

Relate to this situation? See the preregistration [case
study](https://zenodo.org/records/22307709) which provides a number of
strategies to address this kind of barrier.
:::

**How do I know my planned statistical analysis is the right one?**

[Statistics]{style="background-color:  #9854F5; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
To get a better understanding of your real data before your collect it
you can run computer simulations and power analyses. Briefly this
involves:

- Simulating random data with the distribution and sample size of
  expected real data and run the statistical test planned for the study.

- Repeating the statistical test (e.g. 100 x) and check results are
  within the false-positive finding rate of 5%.

- Running a power analysis by simulating data with the expected effect
  size for the study and check model registers effect at least 80% of
  the time.

Take a look at our simulation tutorial
[here](https://lmu-osc.github.io/Introduction-Simulations-in-R/) or a
more beginner friendly guide
[here](https://lmu-osc.github.io/teaching-material-for-novices/open-research-tools/simulations/).
:::

**"Preregistration keeps you in a box"**

[Statistics]{style="background-color:  #9854F5; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}
[Ways of
working]{style="background-color:  #f9c002; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
Preregistrations are sometimes perceived to be restrictive, where you
have to strictly adhere to the study plan. This is not the case!
Preregistrations are a “plan not a prison”, as there are different
degrees of flexibility and you can document any deviations from your
plan when you write up the research findings (DeHaven, 2017).

Preregistrations can also be tailored to the study type (e.g incremental
transparently documenting exploratory-confirmatory pathway or
sequential - multi-stage contingent experiments).

@binney2025a discuss practical guidance of balancing mitigating biases
with flexibility in the research process. @lakens2024 discusses when and
how to deviate from a preregistration.
:::

## Submitting a preregistration

**I forgot to report a statistical test, can I modify my
preregistration?**

[Practical]{style="background-color:  #cc0066; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
Mistakes happen! If you spot the mistake before you carry out your
analysis, you can report a "deviation from preregistration" in a new
document where you transparently describe the change, rationale and
effect of change to the study results (see guidance
[here](https://osf.io/x5w7h/files/yrvcg)).
:::

**I accidentally included sensitive information in my preregistration,
can I withdraw it?**

[Practical]{style="background-color:  #cc0066; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
There are several options depending on when you decide to withdraw your
preregistration:

Depending on the preregistration platform you use, there is an author
approval window after creation of preregistration (2 days for
[OSF](https://help.osf.io/article/330-welcome-to-registrations#Approving-your-Registration-zN2_H),
6 days for [AsPredicted](https://aspredicted.org/messages/edit.php))
where you can cancel it.

If you decide to withdraw after the preregistration is finalized, you
can create a new preregistration with the sensitive information omitted
and document the rationale for withdrawing the original preregistration.
More information about the withdrawal process on
[OSF](https://help.osf.io/article/330-welcome-to-registrations#Withdraw-a-Registration-QWhhB).
:::

## Post preregistration: reporting research

**What sort of things from my preregistration do I need to report in my
manuscript?**

[Practical]{style="background-color:  #cc0066; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}
[Statistics]{style="background-color:  #9854F5; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}
[Study
type]{style="background-color: #2b66ff; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
You will need to reference the preregistrated work in the methods
section of your manuscript by providing a link to the repository. All
the main components of a preregistration (e.g. hypotheses/research
questions, sampling plan, variable description, design plan, outliers
and exceptions, analyses) and any deviations from the preregistration.
You can use this [OSF checklist](https://osf.io/x5w7h/files/zwkqj) to
help you remember what should be reported in your manuscript.
:::

**Where can I find information on which journals accept
preregistrations/registered reports?**

[Practical]{style="background-color:  #cc0066; color: #fcfcfd; padding: 3px 6px; border-radius: 4px;"}

::: {.callout-tip title="Suggestion" collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
There are over 300 journals that adopt the registered report format (see
list of journals
[here](https://www.cos.io/initiatives/registered-reports)).
:::
